modes.name: Short story
modes.job: Tell an invented story in which somebody wants something and something gets in the way.

beats.name: Opening
beats.lookFor: who it is about, where and when, dropped in while something is happening

beats.name: Problem
beats.lookFor: the thing that goes wrong or gets in the way

beats.name: It gets harder
beats.lookFor: at least one attempt that fails or costs something

beats.name: Turning point
beats.lookFor: the moment it is decided, shown rather than summarised

beats.name: Ending
beats.lookFor: what is different now, including inside the character

pitfalls: Starting with waking up and getting dressed
Telling the whole plot in the first paragraph
Ending with "and then I woke up and it was all a dream"
Everything working first try, so nothing is at stake

modes.name: Personal recount
modes.job: Retell something that really happened to you, and say why it mattered.

beats.name: Setting the scene
beats.lookFor: who was there, where, when

beats.name: What happened
beats.lookFor: events in order, the important one slowed down

beats.name: The moment
beats.lookFor: the bit that is the reason for telling it

beats.name: Why it mattered
beats.lookFor: what you thought, felt, or understood afterwards

pitfalls: A list of everything that happened, all at the same speed
"and then... and then... and then"
No sign of why this day is worth telling anyone about

modes.name: Description
modes.job: Put a place, person or moment in front of the reader so clearly they could draw it.

beats.name: The whole picture
beats.lookFor: where we are, in a line or two

beats.name: Close up
beats.lookFor: two or three specific details, not general ones

beats.name: More than seeing
beats.lookFor: sound, smell, touch or temperature

beats.name: The feeling of it
beats.lookFor: the mood the details add up to

pitfalls: Adjective stacking: "the big, old, dark, scary, creepy house"
Naming the feeling instead of showing what causes it
Only what can be seen

modes.name: Persuasive essay or speech
modes.job: Argue one position and bring the reader round to it.

beats.name: Your position
beats.lookFor: what you think, said plainly, early

beats.name: Reason with evidence
beats.lookFor: a reason backed by an example, fact or story

beats.name: Second reason
beats.lookFor: a different reason, not the same one again

beats.name: The other side
beats.lookFor: what someone who disagrees would say

beats.name: Your answer to it
beats.lookFor: why that does not change your position

beats.name: What should happen
beats.lookFor: what you want the reader to do or think now

pitfalls: Saying the same reason three times in different words
Opinion with nothing underneath it
Pretending nobody could disagree
SHOUTING and exclamation marks instead of evidence

modes.name: Discussion essay
modes.job: Weigh both sides fairly, then say where you land and why.

beats.name: The question
beats.lookFor: what is being argued about, and why it matters

beats.name: One side
beats.lookFor: the strongest argument for, with support

beats.name: The other side
beats.lookFor: the strongest argument against, put fairly

beats.name: Weighing up
beats.lookFor: which argument is stronger and why

beats.name: Where you land
beats.lookFor: your own view, earned by what came before

pitfalls: Making one side deliberately weak so the other wins
Never landing anywhere
Two separate essays stapled together with no weighing

forms.name: Advice sheet
forms.audience: someone about to face what you have faced
furniture: A title that says who it is for
pitfalls: Advice so general it helps nobody
Forgetting to say why each tip works

forms.name: Informative guide
forms.audience: a reader who knows nothing about this yet
pitfalls: Assuming the reader already knows
Opinion smuggled in as fact

forms.name: School report
forms.audience: teachers, and the people who read reports
furniture: Sometimes a recommendation at the end
pitfalls: Slang
Sweeping claims with no evidence

forms.name: Newsletter article
forms.audience: families and students at your school
pitfalls: Burying what happened under six lines of throat-clearing

forms.name: Newspaper article
features: The whole story in the first sentence, then detail in falling order of importance
Direct quotes with who said them
pitfalls: The writer’s own opinion
Saving the big news for the end

forms.name: Letter to the editor
forms.audience: the paper, and everyone who reads it
furniture: Sign-off with your name and suburb
features: Names the article or issue it answers
pitfalls: Rudeness instead of argument
Three arguments where one would land

forms.name: Email to an authority
forms.audience: someone with the power to change it
features: Says who you are and why you are writing in the first lines
pitfalls: Never actually asking for anything
Text-message tone

forms.name: Diary entry
features: First person, past tense for events, present for feelings
pitfalls: Writing it as though a stranger will mark it
Events with no feelings attached

forms.name: Review
features: What it is, briefly and without spoiling it
What worked and what did not, with examples
pitfalls: Retelling the whole plot
"It was good" with no evidence

forms.name: Letter to yourself (time capsule)
features: What life is like right now, in detail
pitfalls: Only facts, no voice
Nothing specific enough to be worth reading later

moves.name: Start in the middle
moves.child: Begin while something is already happening, then explain afterwards.

moves.name: Show it, do not say it
moves.child: Instead of naming the feeling, show what the body does.

moves.name: One telling detail
moves.child: One exact detail beats five vague ones.

moves.name: Invented words
moves.child: Make up a word when no real one fits - build it from sounds that feel right.

moves.name: Cliffhanger
moves.child: End a paragraph on the edge, so the reader has to go on.

moves.name: Dialogue that reveals
moves.child: Let what someone says show what they are like, without you explaining it.

moves.name: Long, long, short
moves.child: Two longer sentences, then a very short one. The short one lands.

moves.name: Rule of three
moves.child: Three examples or three words together sound complete.

moves.name: Plain words win
moves.child: Never use a long word where a short one does the job.

moves.name: Give something away
moves.child: Admit the other side has a point, then show why yours still stands. It makes you sound fair.

moves.name: Ask the reader
moves.child: A question the reader answers in their head, on your side.

moves.name: Open with a story
moves.child: Start an argument with one small true story, then widen out.

moves.name: Call back to the start
moves.child: End by touching something from your opening, changed.

moves.name: Wide, then close
moves.child: Show the whole place, then one small thing in it.

moves.name: Slow the important bit
moves.child: Spend the most words on the few seconds that matter most.

moves.name: What could you hear?
moves.child: Add one sound. Most writing forgets sound entirely.

moves.name: Real numbers
moves.child: A number is harder to argue with than "lots".

moves.name: Talk to the reader
moves.child: Say "you" and mean the person reading it.

moves.name: Say less than you mean
moves.child: Playing it down can hit harder than playing it up.

moves.name: Signpost words
moves.child: Small words that tell the reader where they are: firstly, on the other hand, in the end.

moves.name: Put the other side fairly
moves.child: Write the other side as if you believed it. A weak version fools nobody.

moves.name: Because, and so
moves.child: Say what you think, then because, then and so. Three links make an argument.

moves.name: Compare it to something
moves.child: Compare the thing to something the reader already knows.

moves.name: Turn on the last line
moves.child: Save one small surprise or shift of meaning for the final sentence.
